kurals.tamil:
பிறன்பொருளாள் பெட்டொழுகும் பேதைமை ஞாலத்து
அறம்பொருள் கண்டார்கண் இல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Piranporulaal pettozhugum pedhaimai gnaalaththu,
Aramporul kandaarkan il.
kurals.meaning: The foolishness of desiring and pursuing a woman who belongs to another man is never found in those who have truly understood virtue and the right ordering of worldly life.
kurals.elementary: Imagine someone who has studied all the rules of a game very carefully. That person would never try to grab another player's pieces, because they understand how the game works and why the rules matter. This kural says people who really understand what is right and good would never want someone else's husband or wife.
kurals.university: Valluvar opens the chapter by framing adultery first as a failure of intelligence (பேதைமை, 'folly') rather than simply as a sin. The phrase அறம்பொருள் கண்டார் — 'those who have seen aram and porul' — deliberately invokes the first two aims of life that structure the Kural itself (virtue and worldly prosperity), implying that a person who grasps either domain properly would recognise such desire as self-defeating. The word பொருளாள் ('she who is another's porul') reflects the social vocabulary of its age, in which a wife was spoken of as belonging within another's household; modern readers often recast it as a violation of another's committed bond. The kural thus locates the root of the wrong in ignorance, a move that parallels Socratic and Buddhist views that wrongdoing flows from failed understanding.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Let him not show particular attention to an enemy, to the friend of an enemy, to a wicked man, to a thief, or to the wife of another man.”
hinduism.explanation: The Laws of Manu, a classical Hindu code of dharma, lists another man's wife among the people a householder should not seek out or single out for attention.
hinduism.tie_back: Those who have studied dharma (aram) are taught this rule explicitly; the Kural says those who truly understand it never fall into the folly.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Direct dharma-text prohibition; the Kural's specific point about knowledge preventing folly is implied rather than stated.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For this is the will of God, even your sanctification, that ye should abstain from fornication: That every one of you should know how to possess his vessel in sanctification and honour; Not in the lust of concupiscence, even as the Gentiles which know not God.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells believers that sexual self-control is part of knowing God, and contrasts it with the behaviour of those who do not know God.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts tie sexual restraint to knowledge: those who 'know' (God, or aram) do not act on such lust.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong structural match on knowledge versus ignorance; Paul's wording is broader (fornication in general) than the Kural's focus on another's wife.

islam.quote_or_event: “And [also prohibited to you are all] married women except those your right hands possess. [This is] the decree of Allah upon you.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an lists married women among those whom a man is forbidden to seek, calling this a decree of God.
islam.tie_back: Anyone who knows the divine law knows a married woman is off-limits, just as the Kural says those who know aram never pursue another's wife.
islam._accuracy_note: Clear prohibition of married women; the verse is legal rather than about folly or knowledge. Partial excerpt of a longer verse.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's house, thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's wife, nor his manservant, nor his maidservant, nor his ox, nor his ass, nor any thing that is thy neighbour's.”
judaism.explanation: The tenth commandment forbids even desiring a neighbour's wife, listing her among the things that belong within the neighbour's household.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the Torah forbids the desire itself (not only the act), and frames the wife as part of another's household.
judaism._accuracy_note: Near-exact match on coveting another's wife and the household framing; the 'knowledge prevents folly' element is not explicit.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Knowing well these causes of downfall in the world, the noble sage endowed with insight shares a happy realm.”
buddhism.explanation: At the end of a list of the causes of a person's downfall (which includes going to the wives of others), the Buddha says the wise person who understands them avoids ruin.
buddhism.tie_back: The same logic as the Kural: true understanding of what ruins a life keeps the wise from this folly.
buddhism.source: Parabhava Sutta, Sutta Nipata 1.6 (trans. Narada Thera)
buddhism._accuracy_note: The closing verse applies to the whole list of downfalls, of which adultery is one item.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Paris, a Trojan prince, was welcomed as a guest by King Menelaus of Sparta and then carried off Menelaus's wife Helen. In the Iliad (Book 3) his own brother Hector rebukes him as a disgrace, and his act brings war and ruin on all of Troy.
greek_mythology.explanation: Paris had every advantage of rank and upbringing, yet his desire for another man's wife showed a complete lack of good judgement.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Paris is the classic example of the 'folly' the Kural names: a failure to see what virtue and plain self-interest both demand.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrased narrative; strong on folly and its consequences, less on the specific claim about knowledge.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “But most people do not do these, but take refuge in theory and think they are being philosophers and will become good in this way.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle warns that knowing moral theory is not enough; people become good only by actually practising good acts.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar's 'those who have seen aram' are people whose understanding shows in conduct; Aristotle agrees that real ethical knowledge is proven by action.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.4 (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Thematic parallel on knowledge versus conduct; Aristotle does not mention adultery in this passage.

kurals.tamil:
அறன்கடை நின்றாருள் எல்லாம் பிறன்கடை
நின்றாரின் பேதையார் இல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Arankadai nindraarul ellaam pirankadai,
Nindraarin pedhaiyaar il.
kurals.meaning: Of all the people who stand outside the bounds of virtue, none is more foolish than the one who lingers at another man's door, longing for his wife.
kurals.elementary: Think of all the silly, wrong things people can do. This kural says that out of all of them, the silliest is waiting outside a neighbour's house because you want the person who belongs to that family. It is the worst kind of wrong choice.
kurals.university: The couplet turns on a pun with the word கடை, which can mean both 'the outermost/lowest point' and 'a gate or doorway': அறன்கடை ('beyond the edge of virtue') is set against பிறன்கடை ('at another's gate'). Valluvar thus ranks wrongdoers and places the would-be adulterer, loitering at a neighbour's door, at the very bottom for sheer foolishness. The image of standing at the gate stresses both the humiliation of the act and its risk: the man is exposed, waiting, and dependent on another's household. Commentators such as Parimelazhagar read this as a claim that even among sinners this particular vice is uniquely irrational, because it brings danger without any lasting gain.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Ramayana, Ravana, a learned and powerful king, disguises himself as a wandering holy man and comes to the door of the forest hut where Sita, Rama's wife, is alone. He uses the disguise to deceive her and carry her away, which leads to his own destruction.
hinduism.explanation: Ravana literally stands at another man's door, hiding his desire for that man's wife behind a false appearance.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural's image of the fool standing at another's gate, and the epic presents it as the folly that ruined one of the greatest kings.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Narrative paraphrase; the 'standing at the door' detail makes this unusually close to the Kural's image.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Men do not despise a thief, if he steal to satisfy his soul when he is hungry; ... But whoso committeth adultery with a woman lacketh understanding: he that doeth it destroyeth his own soul.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs compares the thief, who at least has an understandable motive, with the adulterer, whom it calls lacking in understanding and self-destructive.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts rank wrongdoers and put the man who pursues another's wife below the others for foolishness.
christianity.source: Proverbs 6:30-32 (KJV), part of the Christian Old Testament
christianity._accuracy_note: Very close: an explicit comparison among wrongdoers that names the adulterer the most senseless. Ellipsis marks omitted verse 31.

islam.quote_or_event: “I asked the Prophet, ‘What is the greatest sin in the Sight of Allah?’ ... I asked, ‘What is next?’ He said, ‘To commit illegal sexual intercourse with the wife of your neighbor.’”
islam.explanation: Asked to rank the greatest sins, the Prophet listed adultery with a neighbour's wife among the three gravest.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, this ranks the pursuit of a neighbour's wife near the very worst of all wrongs.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong match: explicit ranking plus the 'neighbour' detail. Ellipsis marks omitted intermediate question and answer.

judaism.quote_or_event: “If mine heart have been deceived by a woman, or if I have laid wait at my neighbour's door; Then let my wife grind unto another ... For this is an heinous crime; yea, it is an iniquity to be punished by the judges.”
judaism.explanation: Job swears he has never waited at his neighbour's door out of desire, calling such conduct a heinous crime.
judaism.tie_back: Almost the same picture as the Kural: the man lurking at a neighbour's door, judged the worst of offenders.
judaism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one image match ('neighbour's door'). Ellipsis marks omitted words in verse 10.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Not to be contented with one's own wife, and to be seen with harlots and the wives of others — this is a cause of one's downfall.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists pursuing the wives of others among the chief causes that bring a person to ruin.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts rank this conduct among the most self-destructive choices a person can make.
buddhism.source: Parabhava Sutta, Sutta Nipata 1.6 (trans. Narada Thera)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Direct reference to others' wives in a list of downfalls; the Kural's superlative ('none more foolish') is not explicit.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Odyssey, over a hundred suitors spend years in the house of the absent Odysseus, feasting at his expense and pressing his wife Penelope to marry one of them. When Odysseus returns, he and his son kill them all.
greek_mythology.explanation: The suitors linger at another man's hearth, wanting his wife and wasting his goods, until the owner comes home.
greek_mythology.tie_back: They are the Kural's 'those who stand at another's gate' on a grand scale, and the epic judges them the greatest fools of all.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Narrative paraphrase; very close on 'lingering at another's house for his wife', though Penelope's marriage status was uncertain to the suitors.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “But not every action nor every passion admits of a mean; for some have names that already imply badness, e.g. spite, shamelessness, envy, and in the case of actions adultery, theft, murder.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says adultery is not a matter of 'too much or too little'; like theft and murder it is simply bad, always.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle places adultery among the plainly wrong acts; Valluvar goes a step further and calls it the most foolish of them.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.6 (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong on the categorical wrongness of adultery; no explicit ranking as 'most foolish'.

kurals.tamil:
விளிந்தாரின் வேறல்லர் மன்ற தெளிந்தாரில்
தீமை புரிந்துதொழுகு வார்.
kurals.transliteration:
Vilindhaarin verallar mandra thelindhaaril,
Theemai purindhozhugu vaar.
kurals.meaning: Those who plot wrong against the household of people who trust them without doubt are surely no different from the dead.
kurals.elementary: Suppose a friend trusts you so much that they let you into their home anytime. If you used that trust to try to take what is most precious to their family, you would be like a broken, empty person inside, with nothing good left alive in you. That is what this kural says.
kurals.university: The key word தெளிந்தார் means 'those who are clear' or 'those who trust without suspicion': the victims here are friends who have let the man into their home precisely because they do not doubt him. Valluvar's verdict, விளிந்தாரின் வேறல்லர் ('not different from the dead'), is a moral rather than literal death: the betrayer has extinguished what makes a person trustworthy and therefore socially alive. Commentators note the intensifier மன்ற ('certainly'), which removes any softening. The couplet thus adds betrayal of trust to the chapter's charge of folly, anticipating the ancient idea, shared by Stoics and scriptural traditions, that faithlessness destroys the essence of a human being.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “For in this world there is nothing so detrimental to long life as criminal conversation with another man's wife.”
hinduism.explanation: The Laws of Manu say nothing shortens a man's life more than an affair with another man's wife.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts link this wrong with death: Manu speaks of shortened life, Valluvar of a man who is already as good as dead.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong match on the 'death' image; Manu does not mention the betrayal of trust.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But every man is tempted, when he is drawn away of his own lust, and enticed. Then when lust hath conceived, it bringeth forth sin: and sin, when it is finished, bringeth forth death.”
christianity.explanation: James describes how desire grows into sin and how sin, once fully grown, produces death.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural's 'no different from the dead' matches James's picture of lust ending in death.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good on the lust-to-death progression; James speaks of lust in general, not specifically of betraying a trusting friend.

islam.quote_or_event: “And she, in whose house he was, sought to seduce him. She closed the doors and said, ‘Come, you.’ He said, ‘[I seek] the refuge of Allah. Indeed, he is my master, who has made good my residence. Indeed, wrongdoers will not succeed.’”
islam.explanation: When his master's wife tries to seduce him, the prophet Joseph (Yusuf) refuses, pointing to the kindness and trust his master has shown him.
islam.tie_back: Yusuf refuses to do exactly what the Kural condemns, betraying the household of someone who trusted him, and says such wrongdoers cannot succeed.
islam._accuracy_note: Very strong on the betrayal-of-trust element; the 'as good as dead' image is replaced by 'will not succeed'.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Behold, my master wotteth not what is with me in the house, and he hath committed all that he hath to my hand; There is none greater in this house than I; neither hath he kept back any thing from me but thee, because thou art his wife: how then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?”
judaism.explanation: Joseph tells Potiphar's wife that his master has trusted him with everything, and that betraying that trust with her would be a great wickedness.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural's exact situation: the one who is fully trusted in a household refuses to wrong that household.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close match on trust and betrayal; no 'death' imagery.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Just as rust arising from iron eats away the base from which it arises, even so, their own deeds lead transgressors to states of woe.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada compares wrongdoing to rust that eats away the very iron it grows on.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural says the betrayer is hollowed out and lifeless; the Dhammapada says wrong deeds consume the doer from within.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Thematic parallel on self-destruction; the verse does not mention adultery or trust.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Look at Aegisthus; he must needs make love to Agamemnon's wife unrighteously and then kill Agamemnon, though he knew it would be the death of him; for I sent Mercury to warn him not to do either of these things.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Zeus (Jove) explains that Aegisthus seduced King Agamemnon's wife while the king was away at war, and was warned that it would cost him his life.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Aegisthus wronged the household of an absent king and was, in the Kural's words, already a dead man.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong on 'death' and on wronging another's household; Agamemnon's 'trust' in Aegisthus is not stressed in the text.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “How shall I consider you, man? As a neighbour, as a friend? What kind of one? As a citizen? Wherein shall I trust you? So if you were an utensil so worthless that a man could not use you, you would be pitched out on the dung heaps.”
philosophy.explanation: Speaking to a man caught in adultery, Epictetus says the adulterer has made himself impossible to trust, and so useless as a neighbour, friend, or citizen.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar says the betrayer of trust is 'no different from the dead'; Epictetus says he is a useless thing to be thrown away, for the same reason.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Very close on the loss of trust and social 'death'; Epictetus's metaphor is a discarded tool rather than a corpse.

kurals.tamil:
எனைத்துணையர் ஆயினும் என்னாம் தினைத்துணையும்
தேரான் பிறனில் புகல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Enaiththunaiyar aayinum ennaam thinaiththunaiyum,
Theraan piranil pugal.
kurals.meaning: However great a man may be, what is his greatness worth if he enters another man's home for his wife without weighing his wrong even a little?
kurals.elementary: Imagine the best player on a team, who is famous and loved by everyone. If that player cheated in a very unfair way without stopping to think, all their fame would be worth nothing. This kural says the same about a person who goes after someone else's husband or wife: being important cannot save them.
kurals.university: The couplet plays two measures against each other: எனைத்துணை ('however great a measure') and தினைத்துணை ('a millet grain's measure'), the smallest unit in Tamil idiom. A man may possess vast greatness, yet if he does not reflect (தேரான்) for even a millet grain's worth before entering another's home, that greatness is worthless. The rhetorical question என்னாம் ('what does it become?') leaves the answer, nothing, to the listener. The emphasis on failing to reflect links to the chapter's theme of folly: the danger lies in the thoughtless moment in which rank and reputation are thrown away, a pattern visible in stories of kings and heroes across many cultures.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Mahabharata, Kichaka, the powerful commander of King Virata's army, becomes infatuated with Draupadi, the wife of the Pandavas, who is living disguised as a maid at the court. Ignoring her refusals and warnings, he pursues her and is killed at night by Bhima.
hinduism.explanation: Kichaka's power and position did him no good once he recklessly pursued another man's wife.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural's point: however great one is, entering another's home for his wife without a moment's thought ends in ruin.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Virata Parva (narrative summary; trans. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Narrative paraphrase; close on 'greatness undone by thoughtless pursuit of another's wife'.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus asks what worldly success is worth if a person loses their soul in the process.
christianity.tie_back: Same rhetorical move as the Kural: 'however great he may be, what is it worth?' if he destroys himself through wrongdoing.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong structural parallel (a rhetorical question about the worth of greatness); Jesus does not mention adultery here.

islam.quote_or_event: “And do not approach unlawful sexual intercourse. Indeed, it is ever an immorality and is evil as a way.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an forbids not only the act but even approaching it, calling it an evil path.
islam.tie_back: The Kural blames the man who steps into another's home without a moment's reflection; the Qur'an tells believers to stop well before the first step.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong on avoiding the thoughtless first step; the Kural's 'however great' element is absent.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And Nathan said to David, Thou art the man. Thus saith the LORD God of Israel, I anointed thee king over Israel, and I delivered thee out of the hand of Saul; ... thou hast killed Uriah the Hittite with the sword, and hast taken his wife to be thy wife.”
judaism.explanation: The prophet Nathan confronts King David: God had given him a kingdom, yet he took another man's wife and arranged her husband's death.
judaism.tie_back: David is the Kural's 'however great' man: a king whose greatness could not cover his taking of another's wife.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close: the greatest of kings condemned for taking another's wife. Ellipsis marks omitted verse 8 and part of verse 9.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Who plays with dice and drinks intoxicants, goes to women who are dear unto others as their own lives, associates with the mean and not with elders — he declines just as the moon during the waning half.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says that a man who goes to women cherished by others loses his standing, fading away like the waning moon.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts say whatever brightness a man has, he loses it by going after another's cherished wife.
buddhism.source: Sigalovada Sutta, Digha Nikaya 31 (trans. Narada Thera)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close on loss of standing; the verse also lists other vices.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Ill deeds do not prosper, and the weak confound the strong. See how limping Vulcan, lame as he is, has caught Mars who is the fleetest god in heaven.”
greek_mythology.explanation: When Ares (Mars) is caught with Hephaestus's (Vulcan's) wife Aphrodite in a hidden net, the other gods laugh that even the swiftest, strongest god was trapped.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Just as the Kural says, great strength and rank were worth nothing to a god who went after another's wife without thinking.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong match: a mighty god humiliated through adultery; the tone of the episode is comic rather than solemn.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Now in everything the pleasant or pleasure is most to be guarded against; for we do not judge it impartially. We ought, then, to feel towards pleasure as the elders of the people felt towards Helen.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle warns that pleasure clouds our judgement, and says we should treat it as the wise Trojan elders treated Helen: admiring her beauty, yet wishing her sent away to avoid ruin.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural blames the man who does not reflect for even a moment; Aristotle says pleasure is exactly what stops us reflecting, so it must be kept at a distance.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.9 (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Good on the failure to reflect; the Helen allusion links it to adultery, but greatness is not the subject.

kurals.tamil:
எளிதென இல்லிறப்பான் எய்துமெஞ் ஞான்றும்
விளியாது நிற்கும் பழி.
kurals.transliteration:
Elidhena illirappaan eydhum enjnjaandrum,
Viliyaadhu nirkum pazhi.
kurals.meaning: The man who crosses into another's household, thinking it an easy thing, earns a disgrace that never dies and stays with him forever.
kurals.elementary: Some mistakes are like writing on sand: they wash away. Others are like carving into stone: they stay forever. This kural says that going after someone else's husband or wife might seem easy at the time, but the shame is carved in stone and never goes away.
kurals.university: Valluvar contrasts the ease of the act (எளிது, 'easy') with the permanence of its consequence (விளியாது நிற்கும் பழி, 'blame that stands undying'). The verb இல்லிறப்பான் combines இல் ('home') and இறப்பு ('crossing over, transgressing'), so the offender is literally 'one who oversteps a home'. The couplet reflects a culture where reputation (புகழ்) was treated as the only thing that outlives a person, a theme developed in the Kural's later chapter on fame; adultery produces the exact opposite, a lasting infamy. The asymmetry between a moment's ease and an eternity of blame is a common moral argument, found in scriptural warnings about reproach that 'shall not be wiped away'.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Ramayana, Indra, king of the gods, disguises himself as the sage Gautama to approach Gautama's wife Ahalya. The sage discovers him and curses him, and the episode is remembered ever after as a lasting stain on Indra's name.
hinduism.explanation: Even the king of the gods, who thought the deception would be easy, could not escape a disgrace that followed him permanently.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural's 'undying blame': an act taken lightly leaves a mark that never fades.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Narrative paraphrase; versions differ on details of the curse, but the lasting infamy is constant across tellings.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled: but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge.”
christianity.explanation: The letter to the Hebrews says marriage must be kept pure, and that God himself will judge adulterers.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts say what seems easy and hidden will not simply pass: the Kural speaks of lasting blame, Hebrews of divine judgement.
christianity._accuracy_note: Lasting consequence is implied (judgement) rather than stated as permanent public disgrace.

islam.quote_or_event: “And those who do not invoke with Allah another deity or kill the soul which Allah has forbidden [to be killed], except by right, and do not commit unlawful sexual intercourse. And whoever should do that will meet a penalty. Multiplied for him is the punishment on the Day of Resurrection, and he will abide therein humiliated.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an says whoever commits these grave sins, including unlawful intercourse, will face a multiplied penalty and remain in humiliation.
islam.tie_back: The Qur'an's 'abide therein humiliated' echoes the Kural's disgrace that 'never dies'.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong on lasting humiliation; the verses concern the afterlife while the Kural speaks of worldly reputation.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Anyone who descends to Gehenna ultimately ascends, except for three who descend and do not ascend, and these are they: One who engages in intercourse with a married woman ...; and one who humiliates another in public; and one who calls another a derogatory name.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud teaches that most sinners are eventually released from punishment, but someone who commits adultery with a married woman is among the few who never come back out.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts stress permanence: the Kural's blame 'never dies', and in the Talmud the adulterer 'does not ascend'.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 58b (William Davidson / Koren-Steinsaltz translation)
judaism._accuracy_note: Very strong on permanence of consequence; Talmud's frame is punishment after death rather than social disgrace. Ellipsis marks an omitted explanatory clause.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “An evil deed is better left undone, for such a deed torments one afterwards. But a good deed is better done, doing which one repents not later.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says evil deeds keep tormenting the doer long after they are done.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts say that a wrong that seems small at the moment leaves a lasting burden behind.
buddhism._accuracy_note: General teaching on lasting consequences; adultery is not named in this verse (though it appears in the same chapter at verses 309-310).

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Ixion, a king who was a guest at Zeus's own table, tried to seduce Hera, Zeus's wife. As punishment he was bound to a fiery wheel that turns forever, and the poet Pindar says his fate is a lasting warning to all mortals.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ixion thought he could wrong his host's wife and get away with it; instead his punishment became eternal and his name a byword.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Ixion embodies the Kural's 'blame that stands undying': a moment's reckless desire, an eternity of consequence.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Narrative paraphrase; strong on permanence, though Ixion's punishment is eternal torment rather than reputation alone.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “When you have been overcome in sexual intercourse with a person, do not reckon this single defeat only, but reckon that you have also nurtured, increased your incontinence.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus warns that giving in once is never a single event: it strengthens the bad habit and leaves a lasting mark on the character.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural says the 'easy' act leaves a permanent stain on one's name; Epictetus says it leaves a lasting mark on one's soul.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Good on lasting consequence of a moment's lapse; the focus is inner character rather than public reputation.

kurals.tamil:
பகைபாவம் அச்சம் பழியென நான்கும்
இகவாவாம் இல்லிறப்பான் கண்.
kurals.transliteration:
Pagaipaavam achcham pazhiyena naangum,
Igavaavaam illirappaan kan.
kurals.meaning: Enmity, sin, fear, and disgrace: these four never leave the man who transgresses against another's home.
kurals.elementary: Picture someone who takes a thing that belongs to another family. Now four shadows follow them everywhere: people are angry at them, they know they did wrong, they are always scared of being caught, and others think badly of them. This kural says those four shadows never go away.
kurals.university: This couplet is a compact catalogue: பகை (enmity from the wronged husband and his kin), பாவம் (sin, the moral or karmic stain), அச்சம் (constant fear of discovery and revenge), and பழி (public blame). The verb இகவா ('they do not depart') makes all four permanent companions. The list covers the social, spiritual, psychological, and reputational costs of the act, a strikingly complete analysis for two lines. Its closest parallel is Dhammapada 309, which also names exactly four misfortunes for the man who goes to another's wife, a resemblance that scholars have noted when discussing shared ethical currents in early South Asian literature.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “There are three gates leading to the hell of self-destruction for the soul—lust, anger, and greed. Therefore, one should abandon all three.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna names lust first among the three gateways that lead a person to self-destruction.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural lists four evils that follow lust for another's wife; the Gita names lust itself as a gate to ruin.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Shares the enumerated-dangers form and lust as the root; the specific four consequences are not named.

christianity.quote_or_event: “That no man go beyond and defraud his brother in any matter: because that the Lord is the avenger of all such, as we also have forewarned you and testified.”
christianity.explanation: In a passage about sexual purity, Paul warns that anyone who wrongs his brother in this way will face God as avenger.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts say the wrongdoer cannot escape consequences; Paul's 'avenger' corresponds to the Kural's enmity and fear.
christianity._accuracy_note: Covers enmity and fear (divine vengeance) but not the full list of four.

islam.quote_or_event: “When an adulterer commits illegal sexual intercourse, then he is not a believer at the time, he is doing it”
islam.explanation: The Prophet taught that at the moment of committing adultery, the person's faith leaves him.
islam.tie_back: The Kural lists sin among the four things that cling to the adulterer; this hadith shows that sin as the loss of faith itself.
islam._accuracy_note: Covers only the 'sin' element strongly; the other three are not addressed. Quote is the opening clause of a longer hadith (punctuation as in the Sunnah.com translation).

judaism.quote_or_event: “A wound and dishonour shall he get; and his reproach shall not be wiped away. For jealousy is the rage of a man: therefore he will not spare in the day of vengeance. He will not regard any ransom; neither will he rest content, though thou givest many gifts.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs describes what follows adultery: injury, dishonour, lasting reproach, and a husband's jealous fury that no payment can calm.
judaism.tie_back: Nearly the Kural's list: enmity (the husband's rage), fear (no ransom will help), and disgrace (dishonour and reproach).
judaism._accuracy_note: Covers three of the four (enmity, fear, disgrace) explicitly; 'sin' is implied elsewhere in the chapter.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Four misfortunes befall the reckless man who consorts with another's wife: acquisition of demerit, disturbed sleep, ill-repute, and (rebirth in) states of woe.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists four misfortunes for the man who goes to another man's wife: bad karma, sleepless nights, a bad name, and a painful rebirth.
buddhism.tie_back: An almost exact match: four evils that cling to the man, including sin (demerit), fear (disturbed sleep), and disgrace (ill-repute).
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one: same subject, same number (four), three of four items closely correspond.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Alike with him who does wrong to a suppliant or a guest, or who goes up to his brother's bed and commits unnatural sin in lying with his wife, ... truly Zeus himself is angry, and at the last lays on him a heavy requittal for his evil doing.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod warns that a man who lies with his brother's wife earns the anger of Zeus and a heavy punishment in the end.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Hesiod names the enmity of the gods and the sin and punishment that follow; the Kural adds fear and public disgrace to the list.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days, ll. 327-334 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Covers enmity and sin/punishment; 'requittal' is the spelling in the source edition. Ellipsis marks omitted items in Hesiod's list.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “It is just as if the wasps complained because no man cares for them, but all fly from them, and if a man can, he strikes them and knocks them down. You have such a sting that you throw into trouble and pain any man that you wound with it.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus tells the adulterer that he is like a wasp: everyone avoids him, and anyone who can will strike him down.
philosophy.tie_back: This captures the Kural's enmity, fear, and disgrace: the adulterer is shunned, hated, and always in danger.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong on hatred and social rejection; 'sin' in a religious sense is not part of Epictetus's framing.

kurals.tamil:
அறனியலான் இல்வாழ்வான் என்பான் பிறனியலாள்
பெண்மை நயவா தவன்.
kurals.transliteration:
Araniyalaan ilvaazhvaan enbaan piraniyalaal,
Penmai nayavaa thavan.
kurals.meaning: The one who is called a true householder, living by the way of virtue, is the man who does not desire the womanhood of one who belongs to another.
kurals.elementary: What makes someone a good member of a family? This kural gives a simple test: a good family person is happy with their own family and never wishes for someone else's husband or wife. Being loyal is part of being good at home.
kurals.university: Here Valluvar turns from warning to definition: the true இல்வாழ்வான் (householder), the central figure of the whole இல்லறவியல் section, is identified by a negative mark, not desiring பிறனியலாள் ('she who moves within another's sphere'). The word இயல் appears twice, linking அறன்இயலான் ('one whose conduct is shaped by virtue') to பிறன்இயலாள் ('one whose life is joined to another'), so the couplet balances two kinds of belonging. By defining domestic virtue through fidelity, the Kural treats chastity as a duty of husbands as much as of wives, which some modern commentators highlight as notably even-handed for its era. The idea that the good household is built on the spouse's exclusive devotion appears in many traditions' ideals of marriage.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Ramayana, Rama is honoured as ekapatnivrata, a man vowed to one wife. Even when he performs a great royal sacrifice after Sita is gone, he does not remarry but uses a golden image of Sita in her place.
hinduism.explanation: Rama is held up as the ideal householder precisely because his devotion belongs to his wife alone.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural defines the virtuous householder by his fidelity; Rama is the Hindu tradition's model of exactly that.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Narrative paraphrase; the term ekapatnivrata is traditional and widely used for Rama, and the golden-image episode is in the Uttara Kanda.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For this, Thou shalt not commit adultery, Thou shalt not kill, Thou shalt not steal, Thou shalt not bear false witness, Thou shalt not covet; and if there be any other commandment, it is briefly comprehended in this saying, namely, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself. Love worketh no ill to his neighbour.”
christianity.explanation: Paul says all the commandments, starting with the ban on adultery, are summed up in loving one's neighbour.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural's good householder shows his virtue by not wanting his neighbour's wife; Paul says this is simply what love for one's neighbour looks like.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good on fidelity as the mark of a virtuous life; the household focus is less direct.

islam.quote_or_event: “And they who guard their private parts ... But whoever seeks beyond that, then those are the transgressors.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an describes the successful believers as those who guard their chastity except within marriage, and calls anyone who goes beyond this a transgressor.
islam.tie_back: Both texts define the good person by keeping desire within one's own marriage.
islam._accuracy_note: Close on fidelity as the mark of the righteous; verse 23:6 (the exception for spouses) is omitted, marked by the ellipsis.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Drink waters out of thine own cistern, and running waters out of thine own well. ... Let them be only thine own, and not strangers' with thee. Let thy fountain be blessed: and rejoice with the wife of thy youth.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs uses the image of drinking from one's own well to urge a man to find joy only with his own wife.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's ideal householder desires only his own; Proverbs pictures that same faithful household as a blessed fountain.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong on positive marital fidelity; poetic imagery rather than a definition of the householder. Ellipsis marks omitted verse 16.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “In five ways, young householder, should a wife as the West be ministered to by a husband: (i) by being courteous to her, (ii) by not despising her, (iii) by being faithful to her, (iv) by handing over authority to her, (v) by providing her with adornments.”
buddhism.explanation: In his code for lay householders, the Buddha lists faithfulness among a husband's duties to his wife.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts make fidelity a defining duty of the good householder.
buddhism.source: Sigalovada Sutta, Digha Nikaya 31 (trans. Narada Thera)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close: householder ethics with faithfulness as a named duty.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Odysseus finally returns home in the Odyssey, Penelope tests him by asking for their bed to be moved. Odysseus reveals that he built the bed himself around a living olive tree, so it cannot be moved, and she knows he is truly her husband.
greek_mythology.explanation: The immovable marriage bed stands for the unbreakable bond between a faithful husband and wife.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural's true householder keeps his bond whole; Homer's rooted bed is the Greek image of that same faithful home.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong symbol of marital fidelity; Odysseus's own record of fidelity during his travels is imperfect, which weakens the parallel.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “So too we become just by doing just acts, temperate by doing temperate acts, brave by doing brave acts.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says character is built by repeated action: we become temperate by consistently acting with self-control.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural defines the virtuous householder by what he consistently does not desire; Aristotle explains that such character is formed by habit.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.1 (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Weak thematic link on self-controlled character; no direct reference to marriage or another's wife. Best available verified philosophical match.

kurals.tamil:
பிறன்மனை நோக்காத பேராண்மை சான்றோர்க்கு
அறனொன்றோ ஆன்ற வொழுக்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Piranmanai nokkaadha peraanmai saandrorkku,
Aranondro aandra ozhukku.
kurals.meaning: The great manliness that does not even look with desire at another's wife is, for the noble, not merely virtue but the fullness of right conduct.
kurals.elementary: Being truly strong is not about big muscles. This kural says real strength is choosing not even to look at someone else's husband or wife in a wanting way. That kind of self-control is the strongest and best way to behave.
kurals.university: The striking term பேராண்மை ('great manliness' or 'supreme valour') redefines heroism: in a culture that prized martial courage, Valluvar says the greatest valour is the self-mastery not to look (நோக்காத) at another's wife with desire. The couplet moves the moral line from the act to the gaze, the same shift found in the Sermon on the Mount and in the Qur'anic command to lower the gaze. The second line says this restraint is not just one virtue (அறன் ஒன்றோ, 'is it only virtue?') but ஆன்ற ஒழுக்கு, complete or mature conduct, linking this chapter back to the preceding chapter on ஒழுக்கமுடைமை (right conduct). For the சான்றோர் (the noble or accomplished), then, this restraint is the crown of character.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Ramayana, when Rama shows Lakshmana ornaments dropped by the kidnapped Sita, Lakshmana says he cannot recognise her bracelets or earrings, only her anklets, because he bowed at her feet every day and never raised his eyes to look at her.
hinduism.explanation: Lakshmana, a great warrior, had lived beside his brother's wife for years and never once looked at her face with any desire.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural's 'great manliness that does not look at another's wife' in its most famous Indian example.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Narrative paraphrase of a well-known episode; near one-to-one on the refusal to look.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Ye have heard that it was said by them of old time, Thou shalt not commit adultery: But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that the wrong begins with the desiring look, not only with the act.
christianity.tie_back: Same move as the Kural: the line is drawn at the gaze itself.
christianity._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match on the gaze; the Kural adds the idea of restraint as heroism.

islam.quote_or_event: “Tell the believing men to reduce [some] of their vision and guard their private parts. That is purer for them. Indeed, Allah is Acquainted with what they do.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an commands believing men to lower their gaze and guard their chastity.
islam.tie_back: The Kural praises the man who does not look; the Qur'an commands exactly this lowering of the gaze.
islam._accuracy_note: Very close match on restraining the gaze; applies to women generally, not only to another's wife.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I made a covenant with mine eyes; why then should I think upon a maid?”
judaism.explanation: Job says he has made a solemn promise with his own eyes not to look at a woman with desire.
judaism.tie_back: Job's 'covenant with the eyes' is the Kural's refusal to look, framed as a sacred vow.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong on restraint of the gaze; the verse speaks of a young woman ('maid') rather than specifically another's wife.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Come now, monks: with regard to women who are old enough to be your mother, establish the attitude you would have toward your mother. With regard to women who are old enough to be your sister, establish the attitude you'd have toward a sister.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches young monks to look at women as they would at their own mother or sister, so that desire does not arise.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural praises not looking at another's wife with desire; the Buddha trains the eye to see such a woman as family.
buddhism.source: Bharadvaja Sutta, Samyutta Nikaya 35.127 (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong on training the gaze; addressed to celibate monks rather than householders.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Iliad (Book 6), the hero Bellerophon stays as a guest with King Proetus. The king's wife Anteia desires him, but Bellerophon, being honourable, refuses her. She falsely accuses him, and he is sent on deadly quests, which he survives with the gods' help.
greek_mythology.explanation: Bellerophon, famed for his courage, showed an even greater courage by refusing his host's wife.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural's 'great manliness': heroism shown not in battle but in refusing another's wife.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Narrative paraphrase; close match on honourable refusal of another man's wife.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “To-day when I saw a handsome person, I did not say to myself, I wish I could lie with her, and Happy is her husband; for he who says this says, Happy is her adulterer also. Nor do I picture the rest to my mind.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus describes the victory of seeing a beautiful woman and refusing even to let desire or fantasy begin.
philosophy.tie_back: Almost a commentary on the Kural: true strength is not letting the look turn into desire at all.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one: restraint at the level of the gaze and imagination, framed as a victory. Source spells the word 'To—day' with a dash.

kurals.tamil:
நலக்குரியார் யாரெனின் நாமநீர் வைப்பின்
பிறர்க்குரியாள் தோள்தோயா தார்.
kurals.transliteration:
Nalakkuriyaar yaarenin naamaneer vaippin,
Pirarkkuriyaal tholthoyaa thaar.
kurals.meaning: If you ask who, in this world surrounded by the fearsome sea, truly deserves every good thing, it is those who do not embrace a woman who belongs to another.
kurals.elementary: If you asked, 'Who deserves all the best things in the whole wide world?', this kural has an answer: the people who stay loyal and never go after someone else's husband or wife. Being faithful makes you worthy of good things.
kurals.university: The couplet is framed as a question and answer, a device Valluvar uses to give his verdict extra force. The phrase நாமநீர் வைப்பு ('the world set within fearsome waters') is a classical Tamil epithet for the earth encircled by the ocean, so the claim is universal: anywhere in the world. The one worthy of நலம் (goodness, blessing, well-being) is identified by a concrete image, தோள் தோயாதார் ('those whose shoulders do not touch'), an embrace withheld. After several couplets on the ruin that follows adultery, this one reverses the angle and promises reward, showing that the chapter aims to encourage as well as warn.

hinduism.quote_or_event: A widely quoted Sanskrit maxim, usually attributed to Chanakya's Niti, says: one who regards other men's wives as his mother, others' wealth as a lump of clay, and all beings as his own self, is truly wise (a pandita).
hinduism.explanation: This popular saying names respect for other men's wives as the first mark of a truly wise and worthy person.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts answer the question 'who is truly worthy?' by pointing to the person who keeps away from another's wife.
hinduism.source: Chanakya Niti (maxim 'matrvat paradareshu'; paraphrase; verse numbering and attribution vary between editions)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Close thematic match; paraphrased because attribution (Chanakya Niti vs. Hitopadesha and other subhashita collections) and wording vary across editions.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus says the pure-hearted are blessed, and promises them the vision of God.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural says the faithful deserve every good; the Beatitude promises the greatest good to the pure in heart.
christianity._accuracy_note: Parallel on purity bringing blessing; purity here is broader than sexual fidelity.

islam.quote_or_event: “Whoever can guarantee (the chastity of) what is between his two jaw-bones and what is between his two legs (i.e. his tongue and his private parts), I guarantee Paradise for him.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet promised Paradise to anyone who guards his speech and his chastity.
islam.tie_back: The Kural says the chaste deserve all good in the world; the Prophet promises them the highest good of all.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong on chastity rewarded; adds guarding the tongue.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Can a man take fire in his bosom, and his clothes not be burned? Can one go upon hot coals, and his feet not be burned? So he that goeth in to his neighbour's wife; whosoever toucheth her shall not be innocent.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs compares touching a neighbour's wife to carrying fire against one's chest: no one can do it and stay unharmed or innocent.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural praises those who do not 'touch the shoulder' of another's wife; Proverbs says whoever does touch her cannot remain innocent.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close on the 'touch' image, stated negatively (loss of innocence) rather than positively (worthiness of good).

buddhism.quote_or_event: “To support mother and father, to cherish wife and children, and to be engaged in peaceful occupation — this is the greatest blessing.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists caring for one's own spouse and family among the greatest blessings of life.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural ties worthiness of good to faithfulness; the Buddha calls cherishing one's own wife a supreme blessing.
buddhism.source: Maha-mangala Sutta, Sutta Nipata 2.4 (trans. Narada Thera)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Positive counterpart (cherishing one's own wife) rather than direct mention of avoiding another's.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Pindar tells how the hero Peleus, while a guest of King Acastus, was pursued by the king's wife. He refused her out of reverence for Zeus, god of hospitality. After surviving her false accusations, Peleus was rewarded by the gods with marriage to the sea-goddess Thetis, a wedding the gods themselves attended.
greek_mythology.explanation: Peleus refused another man's wife and was rewarded with the greatest honour a mortal could receive.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural's promise exactly: the one who does not embrace another's wife is the one who deserves every good thing.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Narrative paraphrase; very close on refusal followed by reward. Pindar names the queen Hippolyta.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For the man who abstains from bodily pleasures and delights in this very fact is temperate, while the man who is annoyed at it is self-indulgent.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says the truly temperate person is the one who takes joy in holding back from wrong pleasures.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural promises good to those who refrain; Aristotle says the refraining itself becomes a source of joy for the virtuous.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.3 (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Parallel on restraint bringing good; Aristotle speaks of bodily pleasures in general.

kurals.tamil:
அறன்வரையான் அல்ல செயினும் பிறன்வரையாள்
பெண்மை நயவாமை நன்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Aranvaraiyaan alla seyinum piranvaraiyaal,
Penmai nayavaamai nandru.
kurals.meaning: Even if a man lives outside the bounds of virtue and does many wrong things, it is still good that he at least not desire the womanhood of one who lives within another's bounds.
kurals.elementary: Imagine someone who breaks lots of rules. This kural says: even if they have not been good at many things, they should at least keep this one rule and never go after someone else's husband or wife. It is the one line everyone must never cross.
kurals.university: The closing couplet makes a realistic concession: even a man who does not stay within virtue's limits (அறன் வரையான்) and does what should not be done (அல்ல செயினும்) should at least not desire one who lives within another's limits (பிறன் வரையாள்). The repetition of வரை ('boundary') creates a pointed wordplay: he may cross the bounds of virtue, but must not cross the bounds of another's marriage. By holding this line even for the imperfect, Valluvar marks adultery as a floor below which no one should fall, not merely an ideal for saints. The move is pastoral as well as moral, offering even the flawed a place to begin.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Ramayana, Vibhishana, the brother of the demon-king Ravana, belongs to a race known for wrongdoing, yet he repeatedly urges Ravana to return Sita to Rama. When Ravana refuses, Vibhishana leaves him and joins Rama.
hinduism.explanation: Even within a household known for evil deeds, one voice insists that taking another's wife is the line that must not be crossed.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural says even those who do wrong should hold this one line; Vibhishana holds it amid a family of wrongdoers.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Narrative paraphrase; Vibhishana himself is virtuous, so the parallel is to his setting rather than his own conduct.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Flee fornication. Every sin that a man doeth is without the body; but he that committeth fornication sinneth against his own body.”
christianity.explanation: Paul singles out sexual sin as different from all other sins, because it is a sin against one's own body.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts treat this sin as special: whatever else a person does, this one must be fled.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good on singling out sexual sin; Paul's term is broader than adultery with another's wife.

islam.quote_or_event: “Allah will give shade, to seven, on the Day when there will be no shade but His. (These seven persons are) ... a man who refuses the call of a charming woman of noble birth for illicit intercourse with her and says: I am afraid of Allah.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet listed, among seven people God will shelter on Judgement Day, a man who refuses a tempting invitation to sin out of fear of God.
islam.tie_back: Both texts show that holding this one line brings great good, whatever else a person's record may be.
islam._accuracy_note: Close on the value of refusing illicit relations; the hadith does not state the Kural's concession about other wrongdoing. Ellipsis marks omitted items in the list.

judaism.explanation: The seventh commandment states the ban on adultery as an absolute, with no conditions or exceptions.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural sets this as the one line even the imperfect must keep; the Torah states it as a basic, unconditional commandment.
judaism._accuracy_note: Captures the absolute boundary; the Kural's concession for otherwise imperfect people is not present.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Such a man acquires demerit and an unhappy birth in the future. Brief is the pleasure of the frightened man and woman, and the king imposes heavy punishment. Hence, let no man consort with another's wife.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada ends its warning with a plain rule for everyone: no one should go to another man's wife.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural's closing verse, this sets a universal minimum rule that applies to every person.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong universal prohibition; no explicit concession to people who do other wrongs.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Iliad (Book 7), during the war, the Trojan elder Antenor urges his own people to give Helen and her treasure back to the Greeks. Paris agrees to return the treasure but refuses to give up the woman, and the war goes on.
greek_mythology.explanation: Even in the middle of a war, a wise Trojan saw that keeping another man's wife was the wrong at the root of all their suffering.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural marks another's wife as the line not to cross whatever else one does; Antenor saw the same, even though his city did not listen.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Weak-to-moderate parallel on treating another's wife as the non-negotiable wrong; best available Greek narrative match.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Nor does goodness or badness with regard to such things depend on committing adultery with the right woman, at the right time, and in the right way, but simply to do any of them is to go wrong.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says adultery can never be done 'the right way': it is always wrong, whatever the situation.
philosophy.tie_back: Both texts treat adultery as an absolute line: the Kural says even the imperfect must keep it, and Aristotle says no circumstance makes it right.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.6 (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong on adultery as an absolute limit; Aristotle does not make the Kural's concession about other wrongdoing.
